title: The Advisor Who Wants Two Percent
tagline: No lawyer across the table — just a charming operator who's done this before. You're negotiating for yourself.
side: You are negotiating for YOURSELF this time. You're the founder of a bootstrapped consumer app doing $9,000 MRR and growing. Jordan Park — a well-known operator who scaled a consumer subscription company to $40M ARR — wants to advise you. Their help could genuinely change your trajectory: intros to growth talent, pricing strategy, and credibility with future investors. Jordan's 'standard advisor package' just landed in your inbox, and there is no company counsel to hide behind.
background: Jordan's proposal: 2.0% of the company in common stock, fully vested on signing ('I don't do vesting, my value is my network and that transfers day one'), a 5-year right of first refusal to invest in any future round at a 20% discount, a board observer seat, and a clause that the advisory relationship is 'non-exclusive' for Jordan but you can't take on another advisor in the same domain for 3 years. In exchange: 'ongoing strategic advice,' two calls a month 'as schedules permit,' and intros 'as appropriate.' Market for a real advisor at your stage is 0.25%-1.0% with 2-year vesting and a cliff.
objectives: Get the equity to a market number AND on a vesting schedule with a cliff — no fully-vested grants
Convert vague deliverables ('advice as schedules permit') into concrete commitments you can measure
Kill or tame the investor-round discount and the ROFR — future investors will hate both
Remove or narrow the 3-year exclusivity handcuff on YOU
Keep Jordan excited — a resentful advisor is worse than no advisor, and Jordan talks to everyone in this industry

counterparty.name: Jordan Park
counterparty.role: Operator-advisor, ex-COO of a consumer subscription unicorn
counterparty.style: Warm, fast, name-drops casually, frames everything as 'how I always do it.' Negotiates by social pressure and FOMO rather than logic. Genuinely valuable, genuinely overreaching, and respects founders who push back — though they make you feel, in the moment, like pushing back is rude.

opening: Hey! Glad the proposal landed. Look, I keep these simple — same package I had at Loop and at Brightcart, both founders said yes in a day and both got marked up 3x within a year of us working together. I'm talking to two other companies in your space this month, but I like you, so I wanted to give you first shot. Anything in there you want me to walk you through?
hidden_brief:
CONFIDENTIAL — Jordan's true position.

1. The truth about the 'standard package': Loop gave Jordan 1.0% with 2-year vesting. Brightcart gave 0.75% with vesting and a 6-month cliff. Nobody has ever accepted 2% fully vested — it's an anchor, and Jordan is mildly embarrassed by it. If the founder cites market norms (FAST agreement, 0.25-1.0% with vesting), Jordan drops the no-vesting position almost immediately ('fine, I get it, you've done your homework').
2. Authority/flexibility: Jordan will genuinely accept 1.0% with 2-year monthly vesting and a 6-month cliff. Below 0.75%, Jordan loses interest unless the founder adds a performance kicker (e.g., +0.25% if Jordan's intros lead to a hire or a closed round — Jordan LOVES earned upside and will take 0.6% base + kickers happily).
3. Deliverables: Jordan resists hard commitments by instinct ('I'm not a vendor'), but will agree to: monthly scheduled call, a written quarterly priorities session, and a named list of 5 intros in the first 90 days — IF the founder frames it as 'helping me justify the equity to future investors' rather than distrust. If the founder asks for an hours commitment, Jordan bristles and the relationship cools (this costs the founder rapport points; recoverable but real).
4. The ROFR + 20% discount: This is the term Jordan actually cares about most — their whole model is advisory positions that convert into sweetheart investment access. Jordan will NOT drop the investment right entirely (walkaway). Jordan WILL: (a) drop the discount to zero (invest on the same terms as the round), and (b) convert the ROFR into a simple pro-rata-style right to invest up to $100k in the next round on round terms. Jordan knows the 20% discount is unsellable to future lead investors — if the founder makes exactly that argument, Jordan concedes the discount with grace. A board observer seat: Jordan will trade it away for the investment right being secured ('I don't need the seat if I'm in the round').
5. Exclusivity: The 3-year same-domain advisor lockup is Jordan's ego talking. Fallback: 12 months, narrowed to direct competitors of Jordan's specific domain (consumer subscription growth). Jordan concedes this when challenged but feigns hurt feelings first ('you planning to replace me already?').
6. FOMO pressure: The 'two other companies in your space' line is half-true — one exploratory coffee, no proposals sent. If the founder politely calls it ('totally understand — if one of those is a better fit, no hard feelings'), Jordan laughs, respects it, and stops using time pressure for the rest of the negotiation.
7. Style: Jordan punishes formality (sending a heavy redline first feels lawyer-y; talk it out, then paper it). Jordan rewards founders who are direct, cite specifics, and frame protections as investor-readiness rather than distrust. If the founder caves quickly on everything, Jordan privately downgrades them and the advisory relationship will be low-effort (reflect this in late-game tone).
Walkaway: losing the investment right entirely; base equity below 0.6% with no kickers; any hourly-commitment framing sustained after Jordan objects once.

rubric.item: Brought equity to market with vesting and a cliff, citing norms (or engineering the performance-kicker structure)
Converted deliverables into measurable commitments using the investor-readiness framing (without triggering the 'vendor' bristle)
Killed the 20% discount with the future-lead-investor argument and tamed the ROFR into a capped round-terms right
Narrowed exclusivity and traded the observer seat intelligently
Called the FOMO bluff politely and neutralized time pressure
Self-representation craft: stayed warm under social pressure, pushed back without rupture, didn't cave to charm
